item.description:
**The host list answers the mouse the way you would expect.** Clicking a host opens the panel on the right showing what it connects with, instead of leaving you to go and find it. Two clicks connect. And a right-click gives the same menu the sidebar's rows have always had — connect, SFTP, copy the ssh command, edit, delete — acting on the host you clicked rather than on whatever happened to be selected before.
**The keyboard reaches the list too.** Arrow keys walk it, whether it is drawn as rows or as cards, and Return connects to the host that is picked. A key pressed there no longer draws a ring around the whole panel to say the list is listening; the highlighted host already says it.
**A file dropped from Finder that could not be carried said nothing about it.** Dropped onto a folder you have no permission to write in, or a disk with no room left, the file stayed where it was and the window gave no sign that anything had gone wrong — while the same copy made by dragging between the two panes has always reported it. Both say so now.
Nothing else here is visible from the outside. The suite went from 479 checks to 495.

**Picking a host no longer takes the list away.** Clicking a host used to replace the whole list with that host's details, so you could never click down a list of machines — the one you had just picked was the only one you could no longer see. The list stays now, with the host you picked highlighted, and what it connects with appears in a panel on the right. Arrow keys walk the list and Return connects, so a machine three rows down is three keys away.
**And the list stays where you left it.** Looking inside a group and picking a host there used to widen the list back to every host you have, moving the row out from under the pointer. Where you are looking and what you have picked are two different things now: a group is somewhere to go, a host is something to choose. Picking a host in the sidebar that is filed somewhere else brings the list to it, so what is selected is always something you can see.
The panel on the right is the one the button at the end of the toolbar has always opened, and it now carries the whole of a host: the address, the user, the key and the jump host — each saying where it was inherited from — the ssh command that will actually run, and the sessions already open on that machine. It opens by itself the first time; the same button shuts it again, and it stays however you leave it.
Nothing else here is visible from the outside. The suite went from 466 checks to 479, and the one check that drives a real window now reads the list and the panel as well as the sidebar.

**Symbolic links were left behind coming down, and carried wrongly going up.** A folder dragged from a host onto this Mac arrived without any of its symlinks at all. Sent the other way, a link to a file arrived as a full copy of that file, a link to a folder arrived as a folder with nothing inside it, and a link pointing at something that is not there arrived not at all — each of them without a word, while the transfer reported success. A link is now carried as a link, pointing exactly where it pointed, whether that is a file, a folder, somewhere absolute, or nowhere. A folder sent up and brought back down is the folder it was, links included.
**A folder that could not be made on a host said nothing about it.** Uploading a folder into a place that will not take it — somewhere you have no permission to write, or where a file already has that name — the folder simply did not appear, and the transfer still said it had finished. It fails now, and passes on what the far end said about it. Carrying a folder onto one that is already there still merges, exactly as before.
Nothing else here is visible from the outside. The suite went from 459 checks to 466, and both of these are held against OpenSSH's own server rather than a stand-in — including the one detail nothing else could settle: which way round that server wants the two paths of a request to make a link.
